newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street unnerved by military strikes, oil soars.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street unnerved by military strikes, oil soars.

text.p: Stocks and bonds fell sharply Tuesday before bouncing back, and oil prices soared to post-Gulf-War highs on news of U.S. military strikes in Iraq.

The United States launched one of the biggest military strikes against Iraq since the Gulf War, firing 27 cruise missiles at targets in southern Iraq in response to Iraqi attacks on Kurds in the north.
Oil prices jumped as the Iraqi military activity in the Kurdish north prompted the United Nations to freeze plans to allow Iraq to sell $2 billion in oil to pay for food and medical supplies.
"I think Saddam Hussein is testing us," said a trader as stock prices moved broadly lower. Stocks of oil companies and oil drillers bucked the trend and posted gains.
However, a key U.S. economic indicator, the National Association of Purchasing Management index, calmed fears of higher interest rates and took some pressure off Wall Street.
The Dow Jones industrial average dropped more than 50 points just after the start of trading, leading the New York Stock Exchange to put curbs on computerized programme trading.
Blue chips later bounced back, and in early afternoon the Dow was up 18.86 points at 5,635.07.

The Dow came off its early lows after the National Association of Purchasing Management said its index in August rose to 52.6, in line with expectations. A reading above 50 indicates that the manufacturing economy is expanding, while a reading below 50 indicates that activity is contracting.
The news rescued bonds from a sell-off that pushed the yield on the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond to 7.18 percent.
In early afternoon trading the 30-year Treasury bond was up 5/32, reducing the yield to 7.11 percent from 7.12 percent at Friday's close. The U.S. market was closed Monday for the Labour Day holiday.
In lively trading, October crude oil jumped $1.70 to $23.95 a barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange. Oil prices are now at their highest levels since October 1990, when Iraq invaded Kuwait.
Although prices are still below the record high of $40.95 a barrel hit during the Iraqi occupation of Kuwait in 1990, they are $6 higher than at this time last year.
October unleaded gasoline gained 3.49 cents to 65.10 a gallon and heating oil was up 3.28 cents to 66.40 a gallon.
Chevron, Texaco and Exxon, the three oil stocks in the Dow, were each up more than $1 a share in mid-morning.
December gold gave up initial gains at the Commodity Exchange in New York and was down 20 cents an ounce at $391.10.
The dollar rose to 109.26 Japanese yen and 1.4838 German marks from 108.90 yen and 1.4820 marks late Friday.
Financial markets were also nervous ahead of the Sept. 24 meeting of Federal Reserve policy-makers.
"The market is going to be very schizophrenic" between now and the Sept. 24 meeting, said Trude Latimer, an independent analyst.

Lehman Brothers strategist Jeffrey Applegate said the markets were "repricing" for the possibility the Fed will boost short-term rates by half a percentage point instead of the quarter point increase that many had expected.
Marchall Acuff, stategist at Smith Barney, said the Mideast situation "can come and go" as a market factor.
"I don't think at this point that this is the type of thing we were dealing with in the summer of 1990," he said.
"What happened in 1990/91 and what's happening in 1996 are two different events," said William LeFevre of Ehrenkrantz King Nussbaum. "There's not a parallel and don't look for it in the marketplace."

Just prior to the Kuwait invasion, the Dow industrials were around 2,899. The index dipped below 2,400 in October 1990 before ending the year at 2,629. The drop from a mid-1990 peak near 3,000 to the year's low represented a 21 percent decline, LeFevre said.
On Jan. 17, 1991, in response to news that the United States and its allies launched air strikes on Iraq, the Dow rose 114 points to 2,623. It ended 1991 at 3,169.
